title: Likes and dislikes: sentences that flip the subject
goal: Say what you like with two different patterns, name free-time activities, and recognize the "to me … is pleasing" pattern that comes back in unit 17.
bekal: using *Menga … yoqadi* — a pattern whose subject is the thing, not you
using *… ni yaxshi koʻraman* and *… ni yoqtiraman*
turning verbs into nouns with *-(i)sh* to say "like reading"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Boʻsh vaqtingizda nima qilasiz?
dialogs.intro: In the park near the dorm. Nilufar, Budi, and Anvar sit on a bench after class.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Budi, what do you do in your free time?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kitob oʻqishni yoqtiraman. Musiqa ham tinglayman.
lines.id: I like reading books. I also listen to music.
lines.literal: book reading-(object) like-I. music also listen-I.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Qanaqa musiqa? Menga zamonaviy musiqa yoqadi.
lines.id: What kind of music? I like modern music.
lines.literal: what-kind music? me-to modern music pleases.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Menga milliy musiqa koʻproq yoqadi. Dutor tovushi ajoyib.
lines.id: I prefer traditional music. The sound of the dutar is amazing.
lines.literal: me-to national music more pleases. dutar sound-its wonderful.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: And sports? Do you like soccer?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yoqadi, lekin oʻynashni yoqtirmayman. Faqat koʻraman.
lines.id: I do, but I don't like playing. I just watch.
lines.literal: pleases, but playing-(object) like-not-I. only watch-I.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Men esa suzishni yaxshi koʻraman. Har shanba basseynga boraman.
lines.id: As for me, I love swimming. I go to the pool every Saturday.
lines.literal: I as-for swimming-(object) well see-I. every Saturday pool-to go-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: And I don't like cold water!

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Drawing. And walking around the market.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Demak yakshanba kuni uchalamiz bozorga boramiz!
lines.id: So on Sunday the three of us are going to the market!
lines.literal: so Sunday day-its three-of-us market-to go-we!

notes: **Menga yoqadi literally means "to me it is pleasing".** The subject of the sentence is **the thing**, not you — so the verb is always third person: *yoqadi* for one thing, *yoqadilar* for several. The same pattern is used by *kerak* in unit 13 and by aches and pains in unit 17.

**Yoqtirmoq and yaxshi koʻrmoq flip it back.** Here you're the subject, and what you like becomes an object with *-ni*: *Men futbolni yoqtiraman*. Two roads to the same meaning, and Uzbeks use both interchangeably.
**Oʻqishni, oʻynashni, suzishni.** To say "like reading", the verb must first become a noun with *-(i)sh*, then take *-ni*. You already used this *-(i)sh* form in unit 13 for *borishim kerak*.

**Uchalamiz = "the three of us".** From *uch* + *-ala* + a possessive ending. Its cousins: *ikkalamiz* (the two of us), *toʻrtalangiz* (the four of you). A small form that makes a sentence sound warm.

grammars.title: Two ways to say "I like"
body: Both are correct and equally common. What you need to watch is **which endings go where** — swap the patterns and the sentence breaks at once.
after: **Yaxshi koʻrmoq literally means "to see well"** and ranges from "to like" to "to love". Its opposite *yomon koʻrmoq* ("to see badly") = to hate. For love between people, use *sevmoq*: *Men sizni sevaman*.
*Yoqmoq* in the past means "liked (just now)": *Menga film yoqdi* = "I liked the film". It's the most common sentence for giving an opinion after watching or eating something.
⚠️ Don't say *Men yoqaman* for "I like" — it means "I am pleasing (to others)". A very common beginner mistake.

grammars.title: -(i)sh: turning verbs into nouns
body: English just adds "-ing": "I like reading". Uzbek has to turn the verb into a noun first.
after: The rule is the same as for the others: **stem ending in a consonant → -ish; ending in a vowel → -sh.** *yoz-* → *yozish*, but *oʻqi-* → *oʻqi**sh***, *ishla-* → *ishla**sh***.
This form isn't just for likes. It's used wherever you need a noun from a verb: *oʻqish* also means "education", *yozish* means "writing", *turmush qurish* means "marriage".
Combined with *bilmoq*, it means "know how to": *Men suzishni bilaman* = "I can swim" (because I've learned). Compare *suza olaman* in unit 18, which means "I'm able to swim right now".

blocks.text: The opening question to memorize: *Boʻsh vaqtingizda nima qilasiz?* Answer with one of the rows below.

The *dutor* and *doira* are instruments you'll hear everywhere: a plucked two-stringed lute, and a large frame drum played with the hands. *Shashmaqom* music — twelve suites of classical songs from Bukhara — is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, and mentioning it in conversation will pleasantly surprise whoever you're talking to.
Eight short sentences that cover almost every everyday judgment.

*Menimcha* is built from *men* + *-imcha* and means "in my opinion". Its cousins: *sizningcha* (in your opinion), *uningcha* (in his/her opinion). It's the same *-cha* ending that forms language names in unit 6 — here it means "in the way of".

⚠️ *Rozi* comes from the Arabic *rāḍī* (content, satisfied) — the root behind the name "Ridwan". And *Bilmadim* literally means "I didn't know", but it's used for the present too; it sounds softer than *bilmayman*.
